UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Interconnection of Large Loads                             )
to the                                                     )                        Docket No.         RM26-4-000
Interstate Transmission System                             )


                         SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF THE
                   PENNSYLVANIA OFFICE OF CONSUMER ADVOCATE,
                 DELAWARE DIVISION OF THE PUBLIC ADVOCATE, AND
                STATE OF NEW JERSEY, DIVISION OF THE RATE COUNSEL

I.       INTRODUCTION

         The Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate (PA OCA),1 Delaware Division of the

Public Advocate (DE DPA),2 and State of New Jersey, Division of the Rate Counsel3 (collectively,

the Joint Consumer Advocates or JCA) submit these Supplemental Comments4 in response to the

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission’s or FERC’s) Advance Notice of

Proposed Rulemaking (ANOPR)5 in the captioned docket.




1
  The PA OCA represents the interests of Pennsylvania utility consumers before the Commission. See 71 P.S. § 309-4
(outlining powers of Consumer Advocate to represent residential Pennsylvania utility consumers in FERC proceedings
and federal courts).
2
  The DE DPA represents the interests of Delaware regulated utility consumers, including before the Commission.
See 29 Del. C. § 8716(e).
3
  New Jersey Rate Counsel is the administrative agency charged under New Jersey Law with the general protection
of the interests of utility ratepayers. N.J.S.A. § 52:27EE- 46 et seq. Rate Counsel is explicitly empowered to represent
the public interest in federal proceedings. N.J.S.A. §52:27EE-55.
4
  The PA OCA and DE DPA submitted comments and reply comments in this docket. See Joint Consumer Advocate
Comments, PA OCA and DE DPA, RM26-4 (Nov. 21, 2025); see also Joint Consumer Advocate Reply Comments,
PA OCA, DE DPA, and Illinois Attorney General (IL OA), RM26-4 (Dec. 5, 2025).
5
  Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Notice Inviting Comments, Docket
No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 27, 2025) (the Commission issued the ANOPR following a directive from the Secretary of
Energy (“Secretary”) pursuant to section 203 of the Department of Energy Organization Act); see also the full text
of the proposed ANOPR, Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Advance Notice of
Proposed Rulemaking, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (Oct. 23, 2025).

                                                           1
          In the ANOPR, FERC proposed to allocate 100 percent of network upgrade costs to large

load customers.6 In response to this proposal, the following Supplemental Comments have been

submitted in this docket:

             •    March 30, 2026: WIRES’ Supplemental Comments with attached Whitepaper titled
                  “The Risks of Cost Shifts in Serving Large Loads Under a Framework with Direct
                  Allocation of Transmission Costs” (WIRES Whitepaper);7

             •    April 15, 2026: Harvard Electricity Law Initiative’s (ELI’s) Supplemental
                  Comments;8

             •    May 12, 2026: Transmission Access Policy Study Group’s (TAPS’) Supplemental
                  Comments;9

             •    June 6, 2026: FirstEnergy Service Company’s (FirstEnergy’s) Supplemental
                  Comments with attached Whitepaper titled “A Provent Framework for a New
                  American Problem” (FirstEnergy Whitepaper);10 and

             •    June 8, 2026: Maven Solutions’ Supplemental Comments.11

In response to the above-listed Supplemental Comments, the JCA submits these Supplemental

Comments and respectfully requests that the Commission consider these Supplemental Comments

when taking action this month in this docket.12

II.      SUMMARY OF SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF WIRES, HARVARD ELI,
         TAPS, AND FIRSTENERGY

         In the ANOPR, FERC proposed to allocate 100 percent of network upgrade costs to large

load customers.13

            In its Supplemental Comments, WIRES argued that the “the ANOPR proposal to allocate

100 percent of network upgrade costs to large load customers” under a strict application of the

Commission’s “higher of” rate policy creates “the potential for unintended cost shifts to retail

customers under certain implementation scenarios.” WIRES acknowledged the importance of

addressing stranded asset risk (but did not address it) and focused solely on the cost allocation risk

associated within a framework that would solely direct assign the cost of network upgrades to large

load customers, ignoring a disaggregated pricing framework.14

           In response to WIRES, the Harvard ELI directed the Commission toward a potential

“disaggregated” pricing model but did not go so far as to recommend that the Commission

affirmatively adopt such a framework.15 Rather, the Harvard ELI stated that the Commission could

consider a “disaggregated” pricing model and could require utilities to disclose disaggregated

rates.16

           Also, in response to WIRES, TAPS argued that FERC is not restricted to the “higher of”

policy. TAPS argued that FERC developed its “higher of” rate policy decades ago and did not

contemplate the current situation caused by data centers’ surging electricity demands on the grid,

and that FERC has the statutory authority to change its rate policy.17 TAPS cited to the D.C. Circuit,

which explained that the standard for FERC to depart from a past policy “is not an especially high

bar: ‘it suffices that the new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are good reasons for

 it, and that the agency believes it to be better, which the conscious change of course adequately

indicates.’”18,19

         In its Supplemental Comments, FirstEnergy argued that an expansion rate plus embedded

cost rate framework based on the natural gas interstate system (Expansion Rate Policy) does not

raise a concern under FERC’s long-term prohibition on “and pricing”, but even if it does, the “and

pricing” prohibition is FERC policy, not an appellate court-imposed rule. Appellate courts have

addressed the “and pricing” prohibition by saying that “all transmission service…must be provided

at a just and reasonable rate” but they have not categorically adopted a rule requiring FERC to

apply the prohibition.20 Hence, adopting the natural gas framework to electric transmission

infrastructure would require neither statutory change nor a novel assertion of agency authority.21

         The FirstEnergy Whitepaper explains that the Expansion Rate Policy would function as

follows as per the existing natural gas framework (JCA’s clarification additions shown in italics):

              •   The hyperscale data center, electric distributor, and transmission owner would
                  enter into a 15-year or longer agreement;

large load-funding of cost-causer network upgrades. Id. at 7-8, 10-11. First, TAPS argued that FERC must take action
to ensure that retail level protections (e.g., minimum demand charges, minimum contract terms, exit fees, etc.) are
consistently and properly reflected in FERC-jurisdictional transmission rates in all instances and require the parties to
those agreements to clearly identify the impact on other customers before seeking to rely on the Mobile-Sierra
presumption of reasonableness to avoid that presumption from becoming “a straw man behind which the [FERC]
hides to evade its statutory duty of ensuring that the American consumer pays just and reasonable rates.” Id. at 7-8.
Second, TAPS argued that which of the two rate choices – embedded costs with expansion costs rolled in or
incremental expansion costs – is the permissible “higher” one will be case-specific – depending on the magnitude of
incremental costs, the rolled-in transmission rate, the load in question, whether that load is sustained over a long period
of time, etc. Hence, TAPS recommended again the “crediting mechanism” that it advanced in its initial comments as
being both consistent with this “higher of” principle and more protective against cost-shifts caused by large load
interconnections. Under that crediting mechanism, the large load would pay the upfront cost of any network upgrades,
but it would have the opportunity to be credited back that full amount, so long as its transmission usage over time is
sufficient to over the costs. Id. at 10-11.

                share of the existing zonal transmission rate, applying same tariff structure
                applicable to all transmission customers within the zone;

                designed to recover the costs of the network upgrades to the transmission system

     FirstEnergy further argued that additional structural protections could further strengthen this

existing framework, specifically:

            •   The customer’s transmission-rate contribution could be calculated based on the
                higher of actual demand or a minimum contractual demand threshold, preventing
                cost-shifting due to underutilization (good for existing consumers).
            •   Or, expansion rate obligations could be reallocated annually as additional

 III.    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF JCA’S SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

        The Commission should adopt the Expansion Rate Policy set forth in the FirstEnergy

Whitepaper for incremental network upgrades, because it (1) presents a practical and legally

acceptable pathway to ensure just and reasonable rates for all consumers in light of the rapid onset

of voluminous interconnections of hyperscale data center large loads to the interstate transmission

system; and (2) would be the lynchpin to effectuating the Ratepayer Protection Pledge25 as to

interstate transmission wires charges for incremental network upgrades, especially for network

upgrades built as part of Supplemental Projects.26 In the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, prominent




25

https://www.whitehouse.gov/articles/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/; The White House, Fact Sheet: President
Donald J. Trump Advances Energy Affordability with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, March 4, 2026, available at
https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/03/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-advances-energy-affordability-
with-the-ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

PJM OATT, Attach. M-3 § (a).

 hyperscale data center developers promised to “pay for all new power delivery infrastructure

upgrades required to service their data centers, including adequate network upgrade costs to ensure

that these expenses are not passed on to the ordinary household.”27 The Expansion Rate Policy

would effectuate that promise by requiring the large load customer seeking new transmission

capacity to execute a long-term precedent agreement with the transmission owner obligating the

customer to pay distinct charges: first, its pro-rata share of the embedded costs rate for the existing

transmission system; and second, an incremental expansion rate specifically designed to recover

the costs of the new expansion facilities required to serve that customer.28 Such an agreement

would align well with the principle of cost causation and avoid having existing customers subsidize

the costs of network facilities from which existing customers derive no benefit commensurate to

the benefits that large load interconnecting customers derive.29

        FirstEnergy advocates for this two-part rate structure based on a similar existing rate policy

that FERC applies for interstate natural gas pipelines.30 In the interstate natural gas framework, the

Commission has developed an incremental pricing policy to “provide sufficient protection for

captive customers and formally adopted incremental pricing as the default approach for new

expansion projects.”31 Recent appellate decisions have affirmed the Commission’s determination

that the principle of cost causation can be used to assign expansion-related costs to the

corresponding benefit from the network upgrades.32

         The Commission can adopt the Expansion Rate Policy and apply it to incremental

transmission network upgrades notwithstanding any distinctions between interstate pipeline and

interstate transmission facilities. The Commission authorizes expansion facility rates for an

interstate natural gas pipeline if it demonstrates “that rolling in the costs associated with the

construction and operation of new facilities will not result in existing customers subsidizing the

expansion.”33 The network benefits associated with additional marginal capacity on both an

interstate natural gas pipeline system and a high voltage regional transmission grid are, to a large

extent, presumed to inure to all interconnected customers.34 The primary focus of the inquiry across

both industry frameworks is the same: would rolled-in rate treatment force existing customers to

subsidize the construction of expansion facilities? The answer is “yes” for large load customers

interconnecting to the high voltage transmission grid under FERC’s existing policy of charging the

higher of either rolled-in ratemaking treatment (as expanded) or incremental expansion rates.35

         To be clear, rolled-in-rate treatment would force existing customers to subsidize the

construction of expansion facilities. At the same time, requiring large loads to only pay an

incremental rate for the interconnection, as the WIRES Whitepaper emphasizes, results in native

Commission’s “higher-of” policy may insulate native load from near-term harms, but it deprives

native load of the long-term rate benefits from new large load customers.37

        In short, a strict application of FERC’s “higher of” policy no longer protects native

customers from expansion-related costs, as it was initially intended.38 Indeed, current cost

structures require existing customers to unduly bear short-term costs and long-term costs and risks

due to (1) the unique load ramping characteristics of data center large loads,39 and (2) the execution

of electric service agreements that fall far short of the life of installed transmission assets.40

Incremental pricing alone – where the large load pays for expansion facilities – results in large

load customers avoiding the embedded cost of service for existing infrastructure, even though

those facilities benefit the large load customer.41 Immense opportunity exists to benefit existing

transmission customers through large load customers’ paying their share of embedded costs

transmission rates, offsetting already high transmission rates.

        Given the above, the JCA respectfully request that the Commission consider and adopt the

Expansion Rate Policy, as articulated by the FirstEnergy Whitepaper, for network upgrades,

especially for network upgrades built as part of Supplemental Projects.

 IV.     SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

        A.       Summary of FERC’s existing “higher of” rate policy.

        The Commission has adopted a “higher-of” policy for high voltage transmission network

upgrades:

        Under the Commission’s transmission pricing guidelines, a public utility may
        charge the higher of: (1) an average-cost transmission rate reflecting the average
        cost of the transmission grid, including the costs of expanding the grid, or (2) an
        incremental-cost transmission rate reflecting the costs of the particular service
        involved.”). The “higher of” policy effectuates the Commission’s prohibition
        against “and” pricing, under which “the utility is not entitled to charge for both the
        incremental costs of the grid expansion ‘and’ the embedded costs of the grid.”42

        The Commission has a long-standing policy regarding cost allocation for transmission

customers subject to a zonal rate design, that “customers located in each zone pay rates based on

the cost of the transmission facilities located in that zone.”43 Further, that “any degree of integration

in the transmission network is sufficient to establish that a facility is a network facility and that its

costs must be rolled into transmission rates and not directly assigned to specific customers.”44 The

Commission has referred to this as a “presumption” of benefit to the entire system. 45 Under this

framework, the Commission has traditionally examined “the distribution of benefits, not the

original impetus for the project” to ensure compliance with the cost causation principle.46 Though

the JCA acknowledge that the Commission has previously considered and rejected a proposal to

consider network benefits on a customer-by-customer basis,47 this presumption does not hold

under the anticipated size and characteristics of new large load customers.

         Under “[t]he Commission’s long-standing policy [which] ‘favors a roll-in of rates on

integrated transmission systems, absent special circumstances,’”48 the Commission has the

flexibility to determine when special circumstances exist to provide exceptions to this principle.

        B.       FERC should adopt the Expansion Rate Policy for incremental network
                 upgrades caused by large load interconnections and doing so may not require
                 a rate policy change.

        The WIRES Whitepaper shows how the current “higher of” rate policy to meet the needs

of new large load interconnections is insufficient and presumes that there will be no change in

policy. TAPS argues that a new rate policy is needed and well within FERC’s discretion “[g]iven

the new and unique challenges posted by large load interconnections due to their size, rapid pace

of development, and the enormous stranded cost risks they post to other customers.”49

        While FERC certainly has the discretion to change its rate policy in these circumstances,

it may not need to. Under its existing rate policy, the Commission has the flexibility to determine

when special circumstances exist50 to provide exceptions to the “higher of” rate policy. Special

circumstances exist today due to the high volume of large load customers seeking to interconnect

to the transmission system and the speed to power demanded by them, requiring significant

network facilities to be constructed near immediately. These are special circumstances which

require a tailored, flexible approach that is not narrowly constrained by a presumption of system-

wide benefits.

         A broader view of how the benefits of expansion facilities are spread would enable greater

flexibility to protect native load/existing customers.51 A majority of local transmission facility

investment (i.e., Supplemental Projects) to connect and serve new large loads – though nominally

providing system benefits to existing users52 – is not efficient or cost effective for existing

customers. These upgrades distribute more harm than benefit to existing customers, similar to the

D.C. Circuit’s holding in Gas Transmission Nw.53 In the natural gas context, the appellate courts

have affirmed the Commission’s rejection of rolled-in treatment for interstate natural gas

expansion facilities that are caused by an incremental customer interconnections and do not accrue

additional marginal benefits to existing customers.54

        To illustrate further by using a hypothetical, if a transmission utility requested authorization

to build a new switchyard and high voltage transmission lines connecting that switchyard to one

or more existing substations, but where the existing infrastructure is operable and in good condition

– and does not experience and is not forecasted to experience – reliability violations, then the utility

should not be permitted to build that infrastructure. Put simply, this hypothetical scenario is best

described as “gold plating,” and provides only de minimis, cost ineffective marginal value to the

utility’s transmission customers.55 However, this hypothetical is representative of the fact patterns

created by large load customer interconnections where, but-for the large load customer’s

interconnection, there would be no reliability violations requiring new infrastructure. Furthermore,

 the new large load customer may monopolize the incremental transmission capacity needed to

serve them, meaning that the new pathway for electricity that ought to provide reliability and

operational benefits is consumed by the large load customer’s interconnection.56

        Importantly, the cost causation principle applies when, “without the expectation of [a

customer’s] contributions the facilities might not have been built, or might have been delayed.”57

In short, “but-for” the new customer’s interconnection, the facilities might not have been built or

have been delayed to continue to reliably serve existing customers. Where a large load customer’s

interconnection to the transmission system is the “but for” cause for system expansion and/or

network upgrades, native load does not cause the need for such expansion facilities and nothing

indicates that their payment of these incremental costs is necessary to ensure construction of the

expansion facilities in a reasonable amount of time. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge seeks “to

ensure that these expenses are not passed on to the ordinary household.”58 The cost assurance

provided under the Ratepayer Protection Pledge is a strong indication that the largest data center

developers – key drivers of the growth in network expansion facilities – necessitate and can support

direct assignment of the costs of the transmission network upgrades without requiring native

customers to pay for such costs. The Commission’s adoption of the Expansion Rate Policy would

be the lynchpin to effectuating the Ratepayer Protection Pledge as to incremental network

upgrades.59

          Under the Commission’s transmission pricing policy statement, the Commission

specifically endorsed the use of disaggregated incremental pricing and embedded pricing:

         The flexibility that we endorse in this Policy Statement regarding cost
         disaggregation, among other things, addresses the industry’s underlying concerns
         regarding “or” pricing. That is, while we cannot justify pricing that purports to
         recover two measures of a single cost, allowing the entity to account for costs on a
         disaggregated basis would permit separate pricing for separate facilities or small
         groupings of facilities. Hence, we would entertain proposals for flow-based line-
         by-line “or” pricing. This would permit the use of embedded costs for some lines
         when this is the higher of embedded or incremental costs, and the use of incremental
         cost for other lines when this is the higher of embedded or incremental costs.60

The Commission has recently approved a pricing structure which utilized “and” pricing.61

         The Expansion Rate Policy articulated the FirstEnergy Whitepaper is consistent with the

Commission’s Transmission Pricing Policy.62 The Commission’s Transmission Pricing Policy

clearly provides that the use of a disaggregated approach is “or” pricing because it does not charge

the same customer for the same facilities twice.63 Because a line-by-line incremental rate would

exclude the expansion transmission facilities from the embedded network rate base, the large load

customer would be charged once for using the expansion facilities (via the incremental rate) and

once for using the existing transmission network (via the embedded rate).64 Hence, there is no

violation of the prohibition against “and” pricing.65

          C.       If a rate policy change is required, FERC can and should adopt a change.

         If FERC concludes that adopting the Expansion Rate Policy necessitates a change in rate

policy, FERC certainly can and should do so. As FirstEnergy argued, the strict prohibition on “and

pricing” is FERC policy, not an appellate court-imposed rule. Appellate courts have addressed the

“and pricing” prohibition by saying that “all transmission service…must be provided at a just and

reasonable rate” but they have not categorically adopted a rule requiring FERC to apply the

prohibition.66 As TAPS argued, the standard for FERC to depart from a past policy is not an

especially high bar: it suffices that the new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are

good reasons for it, and that the agency believes it to be better, which the conscious change of

course adequately indicates.67

         The bar is met here. As FirstEnergy states, an incremental transmission rate for facilities to

interconnect and serve new large load customers “would require neither statutory change nor a

novel assertion of agency authority.”68 Moreover, there is good reason for it, it will be better for

consumers, and it will be a conscious change of approach. Indeed, the high volume of large load

customers seeking to interconnect to the transmission system and the speed to power demanded

by them, require significant network facilities to be constructed near immediately. At the same

time, current cost structures require existing customers to unduly bear short-term costs and long-

term costs and risks due to (1) the unique load ramping characteristics of data center large loads,69

        The Commission should adopt the Expansion Rate Policy as it will hold native customers

harmless during system expansions built as Supplemental Projects and, to the extent possible,

provide benefits to existing customers as a result of the new load interconnection.77 The

Commission should require transmission owners to adopt a line-by-line incremental pricing

mechanism for the expansion facilities necessary to interconnect and serve new large load

customers and ensure that those customers still contribute to the embedded cost of the high voltage

transmission grid. This paradigm produces the most benefit for native load, without forcing them

to bear inequitable short- and long-term costs or risks associated with those facilities.

        One key feature of the Expansion Rate Policy is providing a negotiated rate structure for

         Maven Solutions’ Supplemental Comments focuses on Order 1920’s architecture for the

proposition that transmission upgrades may benefit the regional grid, which is not applicable to

the incremental network upgrades built as part of Supplemental Projects. At PJM, Order 1000-

based projects are included in the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) under PJM’s

open access transmission tariff and the costs of these projects are allocated on a regional basis,81

whereas Supplemental Projects are included under Attachment M-3 of the same and allocated

entirely intra-zonally.82 Attachment M-3 Supplemental Projects are not subject to the same level

of scrutiny by PJM as RTEP projects,83 but are the types of projects which are designed to meet

customer needs, such as the interconnection and service of new large load customers, and thus can

include network upgrade facilities.84

V.     CONCLUSION

       The Joint Consumer Advocates respectfully request that the Commission consider these

comments. The Expansion Rate Policy (i.e., expansion plus embedded cost framework) is

necessary to effectuate and is consistent with cost causation, the Commission’s existing

Transmission Pricing Policy, and the data center community’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

Therefore, the Joint Consumer Advocates encourage the Commission to affirmatively adopt this

pricing model to be applicable for new large loads and Supplemental Projects when it determines

to undertake further action at this docket.
